rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid-range temperature to capture all 8 compounds, reveal the elution window, and reduce the risk of truncation. This run should show whether peaks are compressed early, stretched late, or still held to the final hold.

All peaks eluted between about 4.1 and 9.4 min in the first run, corresponding roughly to phi_e values near 0.20–0.44, so I am trimming the gradient window tightly around that region to spend the gradient where the peaks are. Keeping tG and T fixed isolates the effect of the narrower phi window on the unresolved 4/5 pair.

The tight window over-compressed much of the mixture, so I am returning to the broad window and doubling tG to test whether the critical unresolved pair is slope-sensitive. This isolates gradient steepness as the main change and should show whether longer gradients can separate the bad pair without exceeding the 10 min target too badly.

The unresolved pair became fully separated at tG 40, so the key pair is strongly slope-sensitive and the optimum should lie between 20 and 40 min. I am testing an intermediate gradient time to recover most of the resolution gain while keeping the last peak near or below 10 min.

The critical pair improves markedly as tG increases, but 24 min was still far from baseline while 40 min overpaid in time, so I am probing the middle at 30 min. This should indicate whether full resolution is reachable near the 10 min cutoff or whether temperature/selectivity changes will be needed.

Since changing slope alone trades one critical pair against another, I am now testing temperature to seek a selectivity shift while keeping the fast 20 min gradient. Lowering T should modestly alter relative retention and may separate the problematic mid-run pair without pushing the last peak past 10 min too far.

At 25 C the separation is nearly ideal, with only one pair slightly below 1.5 and only a small time penalty, so a modest increase in tG may lift that pair over the threshold. This is a local refinement around the current best conditions, changing slope minimally to preserve the favorable selectivity.

The 25 C run suggests temperature is the main selectivity lever, and 22 min achieved full resolution but lost too much on time. I am testing an intermediate temperature at the faster 20 min gradient to see if we can keep the favorable pair separation while pulling the last peak closer to 10 min.

The critical pair shifts strongly with temperature, moving from (3,4) at 25 C to a much worse (2,3) at 30 C, so the optimum is likely close to 25 C rather than higher. I am checking 35 C only to map the selectivity trend cleanly before focusing the remaining search near 25 C with window refinements.

The best point so far is 20 min at 25 C, and 22 min fully resolved but paid too much in time, so the optimum may actually be a slightly shorter run if the near-critical pair stays acceptable. Testing 18 min at 25 C checks whether we can reduce the last peak toward 10 min while retaining most of the favorable selectivity seen at 25 C.

At 25 C and 20 min only one pair is slightly under-resolved, while the last peak is just 0.72 min beyond the 10 min target; lowering phi1 by one step should keep all peaks in-gradient but make the gradient shallower, which may improve the critical pair. This tests whether a small window narrowing can raise the resolution term without a prohibitive time penalty.

A small reduction from phi1 0.95 to 0.90 gave full resolution but too much extra retention, so I am testing a larger window narrowing to see how strongly the critical pair benefits and whether the time penalty scales acceptably. This helps map the phi1 tradeoff around the current best 25 C, 20 min conditions without repeating prior settings.

Lowering phi1 improves resolution but costs too much time, so I am instead raising phi0 one step to narrow the gradient window from the front while keeping late elution strength unchanged. The first peak is still well retained, so this may slightly reduce total retention and redistribute selectivity around the near-critical early-middle pair.

The current best is essentially optimal already, with only one pair just under full credit and the last peak almost exactly at 10 min, so a small increase in tG is the cleanest way to try to push that pair above 1.5. This tests whether full resolution can be achieved with only a very small time penalty from the new best window.

The best method is extremely close to perfect, so the remaining question is whether a small temperature increase with the improved phi0 can preserve full credit on the critical pair while shaving the last peak to 10.0 min or less. This tests a nearby selectivity/time tradeoff around the current optimum without changing the successful gradient shape much.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 gave a major gain with almost no time penalty, so one more step upward may nudge the still-critical pair over 1.5 while keeping the last peak at about 10 min. This is the most promising local refinement around the current best method.

The remaining gap from perfection is tiny, and we have mapped tG and phi-window effects well; the only unexplored local lever around the best window is a larger temperature change. This checks whether the improved phi0 shifts the temperature optimum enough to fully resolve the critical pair while staying under 10 min.

The best method already gives near-perfect resolution and almost no time penalty, so the most plausible remaining improvement is a slight shallowing of the slope from the successful phi0 0.10 window. Reducing phi1 one step may push the 3/4 pair fully over 1.5 while adding only a modest retention increase.

We are very close to the optimum, and the best run missed perfection by only 0.03 min on t_last and a tiny shortfall in one pair, so I am testing a compensating move: lower T for selectivity and shorten tG to recover time. This may keep the favorable 25 C selectivity trend while pulling the last peak back to 10 min or less.

The best run is nearly perfect but misses by a hair on one pair, while reducing phi1 at 20 min fully resolves everything with only a modest time cost. Combining that shallower window with a shorter 18 min gradient may preserve full resolution yet pull t_last back toward 10 min.

Increasing phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 and then 0.15 steadily improved the critical pair while shortening the run, suggesting the optimum may still lie at a slightly higher starting strength. One more step to phi0 0.20 is the best remaining local test to see if the 3/4 pair crosses 1.5 while keeping t_last safely under 10 min.

Higher phi0 shortened the run but eventually hurt the critical pair, while lower phi1 improved that pair but added retention, so the best remaining compromise is to combine the successful directions moderately. This tests whether phi0 0.15 with phi1 0.90 can push the last under-resolved pair over 1.5 while still staying close to the 10 min target.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so the only remaining useful test is whether the method can be shortened while preserving full resolution. Reducing tG by one step is the most direct check for a faster equally optimal method, with the current best retained as fallback.

The current best already achieves the maximum CRF, so only a faster equally optimal variant would matter; increasing temperature is the remaining lever to reduce retention without changing the successful window. This tests whether the fully resolved method can be sped up by temperature while retaining every pair at or above 1.5.

The best method already has CRF 1.000, so the last shot should only test a nearby fully resolved variant that might still score 1.000 with a shorter effective elution window. Lowering phi1 one more step from the winning method is the remaining local change most likely to preserve resolution while checking whether the best window can be tightened further.
